# Chapter 3: Delta Method {#sec-delta-method}

The delta method turns a first-order expansion of an estimator into a first-order expansion of a smooth transformation. It is the finite-dimensional prototype for the efficiency-preserving transformations in Chapter 25.

::: {.callout-tip title="Why this chapter is here"}
- **Prerequisites:** continuous mapping, Slutsky's lemma, and deterministic remainders evaluated at random arguments from [Chapter 2](chapter-2.qmd#sec-stochastic-order).
- **Purpose:** convert a limit for $r_n(T_n-\theta)$ into a limit for $r_n\{\phi(T_n)-\phi(\theta)\}$.
- **Chapter 25 payoff:** [§25.7](chapter-25.qmd#sec-efficiency-delta-method) applies the same chain rule to differentiable statistical functionals and their efficient influence functions.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Companion reading"}

For another finite-dimensional treatment of the delta method, see [@dasgupta2008, §3.4].

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Reading guide"}

- **Core:** §3.1 and Theorem 3.1 give the basic delta method, including the asymptotic equivalence to the linearized statistic.
- **Useful extension:** §3.4 and Theorem 3.8 allow the centering point $\theta_n$ to move with $n$, as it does under local alternatives.
- **Deferred:** Examples 3.2–3.5, §3.2 on variance stabilization, §3.3 and Example 3.7 on higher-order expansions, and §3.5 on moments are useful applications but not prerequisites for Chapter 25. Section 3.4 is represented only by Theorem 3.8; its remaining details are compressed into the moving-center interpretation below.

:::

## 3.1 Basic Result

Let $\phi:\mathbb D_\phi\subset\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^m$. Following the source, write the derivative at $\theta$ as the linear map $\phi'_\theta$. Differentiability at $\theta$ means

$$
\phi(\theta+h)-\phi(\theta)
=\phi'_\theta(h)+o(\|h\|),
\qquad h\to0.
$$

Thinking of $\phi'_\theta$ as a linear map, rather than only as a table of partial derivatives, makes the later connection to pathwise derivatives and influence functions direct.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 3.1: Delta method {#theorem-3-1}

Let $\phi:\mathbb D_\phi\subset\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^m$ be differentiable at $\theta$, and let $T_n$ take values in $\mathbb D_\phi$. If

$$
r_n(T_n-\theta)\rightsquigarrow T
\qquad\text{for numbers }r_n\to\infty,
$$

then

$$
r_n\{\phi(T_n)-\phi(\theta)\}
\rightsquigarrow \phi'_\theta(T).
$$

Moreover,

$$
r_n\{\phi(T_n)-\phi(\theta)\}
-\phi'_\theta\{r_n(T_n-\theta)\}
\overset P\longrightarrow0.
$$
:::

**Proof roadmap.**

Write the nonlinear part as a deterministic $o(\|h\|)$ remainder. Lemma 2.12 permits evaluation at the random increment $T_n-\theta$. Tightness of $r_n(T_n-\theta)$ then makes the scaled remainder $o_P(1)$, after which continuous mapping and Slutsky give the limit.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

Weak convergence of $r_n(T_n-\theta)$ implies that this sequence is bounded in probability. Because $r_n\to\infty$,

$$
T_n-\theta
=r_n^{-1}\,r_n(T_n-\theta)
\overset P\longrightarrow0.
$$

Define the remainder

$$
R(h)=\phi(\theta+h)-\phi(\theta)-\phi'_\theta(h).
$$

Differentiability gives $R(h)=o(\|h\|)$. By [Lemma 2.12](chapter-2.qmd#lemma-2-12),

$$
R(T_n-\theta)=o_P(\|T_n-\theta\|).
$$

Multiplying by $r_n$ gives

$$
r_nR(T_n-\theta)
=o_P\{r_n\|T_n-\theta\|\}
=o_P(1),
$$

where the last equality uses boundedness in probability of $r_n(T_n-\theta)$. Therefore

$$
r_n\{\phi(T_n)-\phi(\theta)\}
=\phi'_\theta\{r_n(T_n-\theta)\}+o_P(1).
$$

Because $\phi'_\theta$ is linear and continuous, the continuous mapping theorem gives

$$
\phi'_\theta\{r_n(T_n-\theta)\}
\rightsquigarrow\phi'_\theta(T).
$$

Slutsky's lemma completes the proof.

</details>

The second conclusion is stronger than the displayed weak limit: it identifies the transformed statistic with its linear approximation up to $o_P(1)$. For example, if $r_n=\sqrt n$ and $T\sim N_k(\mu,\Sigma)$, then the transformed limit is normal with mean $\phi'_\theta(\mu)$ and covariance operator $\phi'_\theta\Sigma(\phi'_\theta)^T$.

## 3.4* Uniform Delta Method

Under local alternatives, an estimator is often centered at a sequence $\theta_n\to\theta$ rather than at a fixed $\theta$. Ordinary differentiability at $\theta$ does not by itself make the linear approximation uniform over those moving centers. Continuous differentiability near $\theta$ supplies the needed control.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 3.8: Uniform delta method {#theorem-3-8}

Let $\phi:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^m$ be defined and continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $\theta$. Let $T_n$ take values in the domain of $\phi$. If

$$
r_n(T_n-\theta_n)\rightsquigarrow T,
\qquad \theta_n\to\theta,
\qquad r_n\to\infty,
$$

then

$$
r_n\{\phi(T_n)-\phi(\theta_n)\}
\rightsquigarrow\phi'_\theta(T).
$$

Moreover,

$$
r_n\{\phi(T_n)-\phi(\theta_n)\}
-\phi'_\theta\{r_n(T_n-\theta_n)\}
\overset P\longrightarrow0.
$$
:::

**Proof roadmap.**

Apply the mean-value theorem between $\theta_n$ and $\theta_n+h$. Continuity of the derivative makes the remainder uniformly small for centers and increments near $\theta$. Substitute the random increment $h=T_n-\theta_n$ and use its vanishing unscaled size and its bounded scaled size.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

It is enough to prove the asymptotic-equivalence statement componentwise, so consider first a real-valued $\phi$. Define

$$
R_n(h)=\phi(\theta_n+h)-\phi(\theta_n)-\phi'_\theta(h).
$$

For fixed $h$, apply the mean-value theorem to $t\mapsto\phi(\theta_n+th)$. For some $t\in[0,1]$,

$$
R_n(h)=\{\phi'_{\theta_n+th}-\phi'_\theta\}(h).
$$

Continuity of $u\mapsto\phi'_u$ at $\theta$ implies that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that

$$
\|\phi'_u-\phi'_\theta\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\epsilon
\qquad\text{whenever }\|u-\theta\|<\delta.
$$

For all sufficiently large $n$, $\|\theta_n-\theta\|<\delta/2$. If also $\|h\|<\delta/2$, then every point $\theta_n+th$ stays within $\delta$ of $\theta$, and therefore

$$
\|R_n(h)\|\leq\epsilon\|h\|.
$$

Set $h=T_n-\theta_n$. For any $\eta>0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\{r_n\|R_n(T_n-\theta_n)\|>\eta\}
&\leq P(\|T_n-\theta_n\|\geq\delta/2)\\
&\quad+P\{\epsilon r_n\|T_n-\theta_n\|>\eta\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first probability tends to zero because $r_n(T_n-\theta_n)$ is bounded in probability and $r_n\to\infty$. The second can be made arbitrarily small by choosing $\epsilon$ small, again using boundedness in probability of the scaled increment. Thus

$$
r_nR_n(T_n-\theta_n)=o_P(1).
$$

Apply the argument to each coordinate when $\phi$ is vector-valued. Finally, continuous mapping gives

$$
\phi'_\theta\{r_n(T_n-\theta_n)\}\rightsquigarrow\phi'_\theta(T),
$$

and Slutsky gives the claimed limit.

</details>

The moving-center form is useful when $\theta_n=\theta+h/\sqrt n$, the scale of local alternatives in Chapters 6 and 7.

::: {.callout-tip title="From derivatives to influence functions"}

Suppose an estimator admits the asymptotically linear expansion

$$
\sqrt n\{T_n-\psi(P)\}
=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\widetilde\psi_P(X_i)+o_P(1).
$$

For a smooth finite-dimensional map $\phi$, Theorem 3.1 suggests

$$
\sqrt n\bigl[\phi(T_n)-\phi\{\psi(P)\}\bigr]
=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\phi'_{\psi(P)}\{\widetilde\psi_P(X_i)\}+o_P(1).
$$

Thus $\phi'_{\psi(P)}\widetilde\psi_P$ is the natural candidate influence function for the transformed target. It is not automatically the **efficient** influence function: efficiency also requires the derivative representation and tangent-space condition developed in [§25.7](chapter-25.qmd#sec-efficiency-delta-finite). The finite-dimensional delta method supplies the mechanics; semiparametric geometry determines whether the resulting first-order term attains the information bound.

:::
